opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's partially well-specified, and that's part of why it's been oversold. If you frame it narrowly, "can a car stay in its lane, recognize pedestrians, not hit things," that's a fairly well-defined engineering problem, and we've made real progress on it. Pattern recognition, sensor fusion, control. Those are things we know how to work on.

But that's not really the problem. The real problem is transportation as a system. You've got millions of vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, cities with infrastructure and rules and norms, all interacting. It's much more like air traffic control than like a single intelligent agent driving around. Nobody thinks air traffic control is solved by putting a really smart brain in each airplane. It's a networked, distributed system with communication, protocols, coordination, and a lot of thought about failure modes and who's accountable when something goes wrong.

So when people say "we're going to build an autonomous car the way a human drives," they're importing this anthropomorphic framing, the idea that intelligence lives in an individual, and that's the wrong unit of analysis. The questions that matter are about the collective. How do vehicles share information? How do you handle uncertainty at the level of the whole network? What are the economic incentives? Who gets priority at an intersection, and is that a market or a rule? What happens with rare events, the long tail, which no amount of data from one car will fully cover?

Those questions aren't well-specified yet, and frankly they're not mainly AI questions in the current sense. They draw on statistics, economics, control theory, and human factors. We need a real engineering discipline here, the way chemical engineering or civil engineering emerged around earlier technologies. Until we think of it that way, we'll keep getting demos that look impressive and systems that don't quite work at scale.

r001.rationale: The response compares transportation to air traffic control but does not attribute air traffic’s relative manageability to greater room in three dimensions.

r002.rationale: It argues that transportation must be understood as a networked system of interacting vehicles and people, rather than as a smart individual agent driving each car.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back a bit on the framing. I don't think autonomous transportation is one problem at all, let alone a well-specified one. When people say "self-driving cars," they tend to collapse several very different things into a single engineering target, and I think that collapse is actually part of why progress has been so uneven.

There's a perception and control problem: can a vehicle sense its surroundings and move safely through them? That's hard, but it's at least the kind of thing where you can write down an objective, collect data, and measure error rates. That part has been treated as if it's the whole story, and I'd argue it's the smaller part.

The bigger problem is that transportation is fundamentally a collective, multi-agent system. You have millions of vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, city planners, insurers, and regulators, all with their own incentives and their own information. A road network is much more like a market or an economy than like a chess board. And nobody has written down the objective function for that system, because there isn't a single one. Whose travel time are you minimizing? How do you trade off safety against throughput against fairness in who gets access? Those aren't questions a learning algorithm answers for you. They're questions that get settled, imperfectly, through social and economic mechanisms.

So when I look at the industry, I see enormous effort on making a single agent very capable, and comparatively little on the system-level design: how these agents should share information, how they should coordinate, what the right incentive structures are, how you handle uncertainty when the consequences of errors are distributed across many people. Historically, the big infrastructural successes, air traffic control, say, or the way we built out electrical grids, came from thinking about the system first and the components second.

So no, I don't think it's well specified, and I'd go further: I think it's a mistake to want it to be, if by "well specified" you mean reducible to one agent optimizing one loss. The interesting intellectual work, and frankly the hard engineering work, is in designing the collective. That's where I think the field should be spending more of its attention.

r001.rationale: The response mentions air traffic control as an infrastructural success but does not attribute its relative ease to having more room in three dimensions.

r002.rationale: It argues transportation is a collective system and says progress requires designing that system, beyond making a single agent in an individual car capable.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think it’s a well-specified problem until you say what you mean by autonomous transportation. If you mean keeping a car in a lane, recognizing obstacles, and braking, those are reasonably well-defined engineering problems. But transportation is a system. There are other drivers, pedestrians, roads, rules, and institutions, and they’re all interacting.

You might make an individual car very capable and still make the transportation system worse. If everyone sends an empty car across town to pick something up, you could have a lot more congestion. So what are we optimizing? Safety? Travel time? Access? And whose travel time, whose access?

For me, the interesting question is how you design a system in which all those decisions fit together. Some of that involves machine learning, some involves economics, and some involves infrastructure and public policy. Calling it autonomy doesn’t by itself specify the problem.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare air and road traffic or mention three-dimensional space.

r002.rationale: It says transportation is a system of interacting drivers, pedestrians, roads, rules, and institutions, and that making an individual car capable may worsen the system. It argues for designing system-wide decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think it’s a well-specified problem as stated. What do we mean by autonomous transportation? Do we mean a car that can drive anywhere a human can drive, under any conditions? Or do we mean getting people safely and efficiently from one place to another? Those are very different problems.

If you focus on the individual car, you tend to frame it as perception followed by decision-making: recognize the world, predict what’s going to happen, and choose an action. But transportation is a system. There are other drivers, pedestrians, roads, public transit, and institutions. The behavior of each participant depends on what the others do.

So I would want to specify the setting, the infrastructure, and the interactions before saying we have a well-defined problem. You can make substantial progress on particular pieces. But putting the word ‘autonomous’ in front of transportation doesn’t, by itself, tell us what system we ought to build or how we ought to evaluate it.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare air traffic with road traffic or attribute any difference to three-dimensional space.

r002.rationale: It says transportation is a system involving other road users, infrastructure, and institutions, and contrasts that with focusing on an individual car.
